claim: Neurotrophins induce fission of mitochondria along embryonic sensory axons.
source: Neurotrophins induce fission of mitochondria along embryonic sensory axons
evidence: This is the main finding stated in the title and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript showing increased fission rates after neurotrophin treatment.

claim: Neurotrophin-induced mitochondrial fission is driven by combined PI3K and Mek-Erk signaling.
source: We report that neurotrophins induce the fission of mitochondria along embryonic chick sensory axons driven by combined PI3K and Mek-Erk signaling.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, which is supported by experimental data showing that inhibition of either PI3K or Mek-Erk prevents NGF-induced fission.

claim: Following an initial burst of fission, a new steady state of neurotrophin-dependent mitochondria length is established.
source: Following an initial burst of fission, a new steady state of neurotrophin-dependent mitochondria length is established.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, which is supported by time-course data showing fission rates return to baseline after initial increase while maintaining altered mitochondrial length and density.

claim: Mek-Erk controls the activity of the fission mediator Drp1 GTPase.
source: Mek-Erk controls the activity of the fission mediator Drp1 GTPase, while PI3K may contribute to the actin-dependent aspect of fission.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, which is supported by data showing Mek-Erk inhibition blocks NGF-induced phosphorylation of Drp1 at S616.

claim: PI3K may contribute to the actin-dependent aspect of fission.
source: Mek-Erk controls the activity of the fission mediator Drp1 GTPase, while PI3K may contribute to the actin-dependent aspect of fission.
evidence: The abstract states this as a possibility, supported by data showing PI3K is required for fission and actin patches, and that actin filaments are required for fission.

claim: Drp1-mediated fission is required for nerve growth factor (NGF)-induced collateral branching in vitro.
source: Drp1-mediated fission is required for nerve growth factor (NGF)-induced collateral branching in vitro and expression of dominant negative Drp1 impairs the branching of axons in the developing spinal cord in vivo.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, which is supported by experimental data showing that inhibition of Drp1 blocks NGF-induced branching.

claim: Expression of dominant negative Drp1 impairs the branching of axons in the developing spinal cord in vivo.
source: Drp1-mediated fission is required for nerve growth factor (NGF)-induced collateral branching in vitro and expression of dominant negative Drp1 impairs the branching of axons in the developing spinal cord in vivo.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, which is supported by in vivo electroporation experiments showing decreased branch density with DNDrp1 expression.

claim: Fission is required for NGF-induced mitochondria-dependent intra-axonal translation of the actin regulatory protein cortactin.
source: Fission is also required for NGF-induced mitochondria-dependent intra-axonal translation of the actin regulatory protein cortactin, a previously determined component of NGF-induced branching.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, which is supported by FRAP experiments and immunocytochemistry showing that inhibition of fission blocks NGF-induced increases in cortactin translation and protein levels.

claim: Cortactin is a previously determined component of NGF-induced branching.
source: Fission is also required for NGF-induced mitochondria-dependent intra-axonal translation of the actin regulatory protein cortactin, a previously determined component of NGF-induced branching.
evidence: The abstract references prior work establishing cortactin's role in NGF-induced branching.

claim: The promotion of axon collateral branching is an important effect of neurotrophin function during both development and nervous system repair.
source: The promotion of axon collateral branching is an important effect of neurotrophin function during both development and nervous system repair (Diamond et al., 1987; Diamond et al., 1992; Cohen-Cory, 1999; Schmidt and Rathjen, 2010; Onifer et al., 2011; Bilimoria and Bonni, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: In the context of axon branching, neurotrophins regulate both the actin filament and microtubule cytoskeleton.
source: In the context of axon branching, neurotophins regulate both the actin filament and microtubule cytoskeleton (Kalil and Dent, 2014; Armijo-Weingart and Gallo, 2017) and also drive the intra-axonal translation of mRNAs coding for actin regulatory proteins involved in branching (Spillane et al., 2012; Batista and Hengst, 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Neurotrophins drive the intra-axonal translation of mRNAs coding for actin regulatory proteins involved in branching.
source: In the context of axon branching, neurotophins regulate both the actin filament and microtubule cytoskeleton (Kalil and Dent, 2014; Armijo-Weingart and Gallo, 2017) and also drive the intra-axonal translation of mRNAs coding for actin regulatory proteins involved in branching (Spillane et al., 2012; Batista and Hengst, 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Recent work has identified mitochondria as fundamental elements in the mechanism of branching.
source: Recent work has identified mitochondria as fundamental elements in the mechanism of branching (Courchet et al., 2013; Spillane et al., 2013; Tao et al., 2014; Sainath et al., 2017a; Wong et al., 2017; Smith and Gallo, 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to recent literature.

claim: During NGF-induced branching mitochondrial respiration serves to locally drive axonal actin dynamics and intra-axonal translation of actin regulatory proteins required for NGF-induced branching.
source: During NGF-induced branching mitochondrial respiration serves to locally drive axonal actin dynamics and intra-axonal translation of actin regulatory proteins required for NGF-induced branching (Ketschek and Gallo, 2010; Spillane et al., 2012; Spillane et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Prior work has determined that neurotrophins can regulate stalling at sites of localized NGF-signaling, mitochondrial membrane potential and coordinate axonal actin dynamics and mitochondria positioning.
source: Prior work has determined that neurotrophins can regulate stalling at sites of localized NGF-signaling, mitochondrial membrane potential and coordinate axonal actin dynamics and mitochondria positioning (Chada and Hollenbeck, 2004; Verburg and Hollenbeck, 2008; Ketschek and Gallo, 2010; Spillane et al., 2013; Sainath et al., 2017a).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Mitochondria are dynamic organelles that undergo fission and fusion in axons.
source: Mitochondria are dynamic organelles that undergo fission and fusion in axons (Amiri and Hollenbeck, 2008; Saxton and Hollenbeck, 2012; Smith and Gallo, 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The balance of fission and fusion serves to maintain cellular health, and fission positively contributes to aspects of cell division and organismal development.
source: The balance of fission and fusion serves to maintain cellular health, and fission positively contributes to aspects of cell division and organismal development.
evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge about mitochondrial dynamics.

claim: Fission is a characteristic response to a variety of insults and is generally considered to be a component of the cell death mechanism that when left unchecked results in fragmentation of mitochondria and loss of function.
source: However, fission is also a characteristic response to a variety of insults and is generally considered to be a component of the cell death mechanism that when left unchecked results in fragmentation of mitochondria and loss of function (Balog et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation and reflects established knowledge.

claim: Dysregulation of the fission-fusion balance is considered to underlie certain neuropathies and to have detrimental effects on neuronal health.
source: Dysregulation of the fission-fusion balance is also considered to underlie certain neuropathies and to have detrimental effects on neuronal health (Bertholet et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: NGF treatment elevated rates of fission without detectable effects on the rate of fusion during the first 10 min.
source: Imaging of fluorescently labeled mitochondria during the first 10 min after NGF treatment revealed elevated rates of fission (% mitochondria undergoing fission/10 min) without detectable effects on the rate of fusion (Figure 1A,B) relative to the no NGF treatment control (NGF vehicle treatment).
evidence: This claim is supported by live imaging data presented in Figure 1A,B.

claim: In 80% of instances of fission one or both of the emergent mitochondria underwent transport.
source: In 80% of instances of fission one or both of the emergent mitochondria underwent transport (see Figure 1A for an example of transport following fission; Figure 1—figure supplement 1 shows an example of fission without subsequent transport), regardless of NGF treatment (p=0.56, Fisher's test).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of live imaging data.

claim: Fission correlates with an increased probability of subsequent transport regardless of NGF treatment.
source: Thus, fission correlates with an increased probability of subsequent transport regardless of NGF treatment.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data showing 80% of mitochondria undergo transport after fission.

claim: Fission occurred along stalled mitochondria and moving mitochondria were not observed undergoing fission.
source: Fission occurred along stalled mitochondria and we did not observe moving mitochondria undergoing fission.
evidence: This is a direct observation from live imaging experiments.

claim: The proportion of mitochondria undergoing transport after fission was 110% greater than that of other mitochondria that were initially stalled but then underwent transport without having undergone fission.
source: The proportion of mitochondria undergoing transport after fission was 110% greater than that of other mitochondria that were initially stalled but then underwent transport without having undergone fission (80% following fission relative to 38% not having undergone fission; p=0.0025. Fisher's test).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis with statistical testing.

claim: During the first 10 min of NGF treatment there was a trend toward increased transport as reflected in a slight decrease in the % of mitochondria that remained stalled throughout the imaging.
source: Considering the whole population of axonal mitochondria, during the first 10 min of NGF treatment there was a trend toward increased transport as reflected in a slight decrease in the % of mitochondria that remained stalled throughout the imaging (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), likely due to the proportion having undergone fission.
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and includes an inference about the cause.

claim: The percent of time that mitochondria which underwent movement spent moving was not affected by NGF for either anterograde or retrograde directions.
source: The percent of time that mitochondria which underwent movement spent moving was not affected by NGF for either anterograde or retrograde directions (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A inset).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A inset.

claim: For mitochondria having undergone fission after NGF treatment the transport was not biased in the anterograde or retrograde direction.
source: For mitochondria having undergone fission after NGF treatment the transport was not biased in the anterograde or retrograde direction (p=0.29; Fisher's test against a hypothetical population of the same sample size exhibiting 50/50 directionality) and the velocity of movement in either direction was not affected by NGF treatment (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of transport directionality data.

claim: The velocity of movement in either direction was not affected by NGF treatment for mitochondria having undergone fission.
source: For mitochondria having undergone fission after NGF treatment the transport was not biased in the anterograde or retrograde direction (p=0.29; Fisher's test against a hypothetical population of the same sample size exhibiting 50/50 directionality) and the velocity of movement in either direction was not affected by NGF treatment (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The velocity of transport in either direction was not affected by NGF between moving mitochondria not observed to have undergone fission and those that underwent fission prior to transport.
source: The velocity of transport in either direction was also not affected by NGF between moving mitochondria not observed to have undergone fission and those that underwent fission prior to transport (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Analysis of the 'run length' did not reveal an effect of NGF.
source: Analysis of the 'run length', the net distance traveled by mitochondria during a continuous period of transport, did not reveal an effect of NGF (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C), although in the no NGF group we observed a trend toward more mitochondria undergoing continuous runs longer than 35 microns in either direction.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Following NGF treatment 55% of mitochondria undergoing runs exhibited one or more switches in direction during the run, compared to 15% in the no NGF group.
source: However, following NGF treatment 55% of mitochondria undergoing runs exhibited one or more switches in direction during the run, compared to 15% in the no NGF group (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D; n = 47 and 38 respectively, p=0.0049, Fisher exact test).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data with statistical testing.

claim: NGF treatment results in mitochondria undergoing transport exhibiting more frequent reversal of directionality during a continuous run.
source: Thus, NGF treatment results in a bout of fission following which one or both of the two emergent mitochondria undergo redistribution within the axon, the latter correlating with fission and not linked to NGF-treatment. Although NGF did not impact a variety of aspects of mitochondria transport, in response to NGF the mitochondria undergoing transport exhibited more frequent reversal of directionality during a continuous run.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the data on directional switches during runs.

claim: A 15-45 min treatment with NGF increased the density of axonal mitochondria and decreased their length.
source: Consistent with the bout of fission observed in live imaging studies during the first 10 min of NGF treatment, analysis of the density and length of axonal mitochondria in axons at 15–45 min following treatment with NGF revealed increased density (mitochondria/unit length of axon) of shorter mitochondria, an effect persistent after 15 min post treatment and also observed when neurons were cultured in the presence of NGF overnight (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2E.

claim: The effect of NGF on mitochondria length and density was persistent after 15 min post treatment and also observed when neurons were cultured in the presence of NGF overnight.
source: Consistent with the bout of fission observed in live imaging studies during the first 10 min of NGF treatment, analysis of the density and length of axonal mitochondria in axons at 15–45 min following treatment with NGF revealed increased density (mitochondria/unit length of axon) of shorter mitochondria, an effect persistent after 15 min post treatment and also observed when neurons were cultured in the presence of NGF overnight (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by time-course data in Figure 1C.

claim: Analysis of the rates of fission and fusion at 1 hr post NGF treatment did not reveal an effect of NGF.
source: Consistent with a maintained new steady state of length and density by 15 min after NGF treatment, analysis of the rates of fission and fusion at 1 hr post NGF treatment (during a 10 min period for direct comparison to Figure 1B) did not reveal an effect of NGF (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data in Figure 1D.

claim: In no NGF and 1 hr NGF conditions the rates of fission matched those of fusion, as expected for maintenance of the population of mitochondria length at steady state.
source: In no NGF and 1 hr NGF conditions the rates of fission matched those of fusion, as expected for maintenance of the population of mitochondria length at steady state.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data in Figure 1D based on the principle that balanced fission and fusion maintain steady state.

claim: The initial burst of fission during the 0–10 min of NGF treatment is no longer detectable by 1 hr after NGF treatment.
source: Thus, the initial burst of fission during the 0–10 min of NGF treatment is no longer detectable by 1 hr after NGF treatment and the percentage of mitochondria undergoing fission has returned to baseline (no NGF treatment) levels, which do not differ at 0–10 and 60–70 min.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis comparing fission rates at different time points.

claim: A 45 min treatment with BDNF or NT3 increased the density of axonal mitochondria and decreased their length.
source: As with NGF, a 45 min treatment with BDNF or NT3 increased the density of axonal mitochondria and decreased their length (Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 2F.

claim: Following NGF withdraw mitochondria length and density increased and decreased, respectively, back to NO NGF treatment levels by 3 hr.
source: Following NGF withdraw mitochondria length and density increased and decreased, respectively, back to NO NGF treatment levels by 3 hr (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data in Figure 1F.

claim: Analysis of the percentage of mitochondria undergoing fission or fusion after NGF withdraw revealed increased rates of fusion at 10–20 min after NGF withdraw which returned to baseline by 40–50 min after NGF withdraw.
source: Analysis of the percentage of mitochondria undergoing fission or fusion (as in Figure 1B,D) after NGF withdraw in the same paradigm as in Figure 1F revealed increased rates of fusion at 10–20 min after NGF withdraw which returned to baseline by 40–50 min after NGF withdraw (Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data in Figure 1G.

claim: NGF withdraw did not affect rates of fission at either time points after withdrawal.
source: NGF withdraw did not affect rates of fission at either time points.
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 1G showing no change in fission rates.

claim: Loss of NGF signaling after a period of NGF signaling results in a bout of fusion.
source: Thus, loss of NGF signaling after a period of NGF signaling results in a bout of fusion.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the data showing increased fusion after NGF withdrawal.

claim: By 40–50 min after NGF withdraw the rates of fission and fusion are comparable, consistent with the maintenance of steady state induced by NGF withdraw.
source: However, by 40–50 min after NGF withdraw the rates of fission and fusion are comparable (p=0.91, Mann-Whintey test), consistent with the maintenance of steady state induced by NGF withdraw.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of fission and fusion rates.

claim: NGF induces the fission of axonal mitochondria and determines a new steady state of length and density that is then maintained as long as NGF is present.
source: Collectively, these data reveal that NGF induces the fission of axonal mitochondria and determines a new steady state of length and density that is then maintained as long as NGF is present.
evidence: This is a summary statement integrating multiple experimental findings.

claim: The time course of fission in response to bath application of NGF (<10 min) indicates that the response is mediated locally within the axon shaft.
source: The time course of fission in response to bath application of NGF (<10 min) indicates that the response is mediated locally within the axon shaft.
evidence: This is an inference based on the rapid time course of the response.

claim: During the first 10 min of local perfusion with NGF an average of 30% of mitochondria underwent fission, similar to bath application.
source: During the first 10 min of local perfusion with NGF an average of 30% of mitochondria underwent fission (Figure 1—figure supplement 2H), similar to bath application (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data from local perfusion experiments.

claim: Local perfusion with NGF did not affect the percentage of mitochondria undergoing fusion.
source: As with bath application, we did not observe an effect of local perfusion with NGF on the percentage of mitochondria undergoing fusion (Figure 1—figure supplement 2H).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data from local perfusion experiments.

claim: Axons in compartments containing NGF exhibited shorter mitochondria relative to no NGF.
source: Axons in compartments containing NGF exhibited shorter mitochondria relative to no NGF (Figure 1—figure supplement 2I), consistent with a local action of NGF.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data from microfluidic chamber experiments.

claim: The effect of NGF on mitochondria length and density became evident at 10 ng/mL NGF.
source: A dose response curve showed that the effect of NGF on mitochondria length and density became evident at 10 ng/mL NGF (Figure 1—figure supplement 2J), consistent with activation of TrkA receptors.
evidence: This claim is supported by dose-response data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2J.

claim: Pretreatment with the TrkA inhibitor k252a prior to NGF treatment resulted in inhibition of the NGF-induced decrease in mitochondria length.
source: To further address the issue we pretreated with the TrkA inhibitor k252a prior to NGF treatment resulting in inhibition of the NGF-induced decrease in mitochondria length (Figure 1—figure supplement 2K).
evidence: This claim is supported by pharmacological inhibition data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2K.

claim: Treatment with BDNF (100 ng/mL) did not alter mitochondria length in axons of neurons cultured in no NGF.
source: All neurotrophins bind the p75 receptor but exhibit selectivity for Trk receptors. Treatment with BDNF (100 ng/mL) did not alter mitochondria length (Figure 1—figure supplement 2K).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2K.

claim: The effects of NGF on axonal mitochondria are mediated through the TrkA receptor.
source: Collectively, these data indicate the effects of NGF on axonal mitochondria are mediated through the TrkA receptor.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on dose-response, k252a inhibition, and BDNF treatment data.

claim: Drp1 mediates fission in toxic scenarios as well as baseline fission in a variety of cell types.
source: Drp1 mediates fission in toxic scenarios as well as baseline fission in a variety of cell types (Zemirli et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Oligomers of Drp1 accumulate at the site of fission and form a ring around the mitochondrion.
source: Oligomers of Drp1 accumulate at the site of fission and form a ring around the mitochondrion (Hatch et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Endogenous Drp1 was found throughout axons exhibiting a punctate distribution and puncta of Drp1 colocalized with the ends of closely apposed mitochondria.
source: As revealed by immunocytochemistry endogenous Drp1 was found throughout axons exhibiting a punctate distribution and puncta of Drp1 colocalized with the ends of closely apposed mitochondria that may be reflective of having undergone fission around the time of fixation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunocytochemistry data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: Sites of eventual fission were demarcated by the prior focal accumulation of Drp1.
source: Sites of eventual fission were demarcated by the prior focal accumulation of Drp1 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by live imaging data in Figure 2A.

claim: Treatment with NGF increased the frequency of Drp1 focal accumulation along mitochondria.
source: Treatment with NGF increased the frequency of Drp1 focal accumulation along mitochondria (Figure 2B), consistent with its role in promoting fission.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data in Figure 2B.

claim: Inhibition of Drp1 activity using mDivi-1, P110, or expression of dominant negative Drp1 blocked the effects of NGF on mitochondria fission.
source: Inhibition of Drp1 activity using the pharmacological inhibitor mDivi-1 (Figure 2C; Cassidy-Stone et al., 2008; Smith and Gallo, 2017), the P110 cell permeable Drp1 inhibitory peptide (Figure 2C; Qi et al., 2013) or expression of dominant negative (DN) Drp1 (Figure 2D, inset shows an example of DNDrp1 expression and targeting to mitochondria; Stojanovski et al., 2004; Barsoum et al., 2006) blocked the effects of NGF on mitochondria fission.
evidence: This claim is supported by pharmacological and genetic inhibition data in Figure 2C and 2D.

claim: Overnight expression of DNDrp1 in the absence of NGF increased mitochondria lengths and decreased densities.
source: Overnight expression of DNDrp1 in the absence of NGF increased mitochondria lengths and decreased densities (Figure 2E), as expected.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data in Figure 2E.

claim: Actin filaments are emerging as a component of the fission mechanism.
source: Actin filaments are emerging as a component of the fission mechanism (Hatch et al., 2014; Kraus and Ryan, 2017), and NGF upregulates axonal actin dynamics reflected in localized dynamic patches of filaments (Loudon et al., 2006; Ketschek and Gallo, 2010; Spillane et al., 2011; Spillane et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to recent literature.

claim: NGF upregulates axonal actin dynamics reflected in localized dynamic patches of filaments.
source: Actin filaments are emerging as a component of the fission mechanism (Hatch et al., 2014; Kraus and Ryan, 2017), and NGF upregulates axonal actin dynamics reflected in localized dynamic patches of filaments (Loudon et al., 2006; Ketschek and Gallo, 2010; Spillane et al., 2011; Spillane et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Sites of fission correlated with the presence of actin patches along the mitochondrion.
source: Imaging of eYFP-β-actin revealed that sites of fission correlated with the presence of actin patches along the mitochondrion (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by live imaging data in Figure 3A.

claim: 80% of fission sites colocalized with detectable actin patches.
source: We observed 80% of fission sites (n = 25; 20/25 sites) colocalizing with detectable actin patches.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of live imaging data.

claim: Based on empirical data, the probability of observing the detected 20 instances of overlap between actin filament patches and sites of fission is 1.75 × 10−21.
source: Based on these empirical data, the probability of observing the detected the observed 20 instances of overlap between actin filament patches and sites of fission in this data set is 1.75 × 10−21.
evidence: This is a calculated probability based on the empirical data in Table 1.

claim: Pretreatment with latrunculin-A blocked the promotion of fission by NGF.
source: To address whether actin filaments colocalizing with sites of fission may have a role in fission, we depolymerized actin filaments using latrunuclin-A prior to treatment with NGF. Latrunculin-A blocked the promotion of fission by NGF (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) without affecting fusion (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by pharmacological inhibition data in Figure 3B.

claim: Latrunculin-A did not affect fusion.
source: Latrunculin-A blocked the promotion of fission by NGF (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) without affecting fusion (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Treatment with latrunculin A blocked the NGF-induced increase in the formation of Drp1-puncta along mitochondria.
source: Furthermore, treatment with latrunculin A blocked the NGF-induced increase in the formation of Drp1-puncta along mitochondria (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data in Figure 3C.

claim: The mechanism of NGF-induced fission requires the combined activity of the Drp1 GTPase and actin filaments, the latter being required for the formation of focal accumulations of Drp1 along mitochondria.
source: Collectively, the data indicate that the mechanism of NGF-induced fission requires the combined activity of the Drp1 GTPase and actin filaments, the latter being required for the formation of focal accumulations of Drp1 along mitochondria.
evidence: This is a summary statement integrating multiple experimental findings.

claim: Axonal actin patches have a previously described role in serving as cytoskeletal platforms for the emergence of axonal filopodia.
source: Axonal actin patches have a previously described role in serving as cytoskeletal platforms for the emergence of axonal filopodia (Figure 3D; Loudon et al., 2006; Ketschek and Gallo, 2010; Hand et al., 2015; Ketschek et al., 2016) and the emergence of filopodia occurs preferentially from patches associated with mitochondria (Figure 3D; Spillane et al., 2013; Sainath et al., 2017a).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The emergence of filopodia occurs preferentially from patches associated with mitochondria.
source: Axonal actin patches have a previously described role in serving as cytoskeletal platforms for the emergence of axonal filopodia (Figure 3D; Loudon et al., 2006; Ketschek and Gallo, 2010; Hand et al., 2015; Ketschek et al., 2016) and the emergence of filopodia occurs preferentially from patches associated with mitochondria (Figure 3D; Spillane et al., 2013; Sainath et al., 2017a).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Patches associated with sites of fission are longer in duration than those that arise at sites colocalizing with mitochondria but not associated with fission sites, and also those that arise at non-mitochondrial sites along the axon.
source: Analysis of the duration of patches during the first 10 min of NGF treatment revealed that patches associated with sites of fission are longer in duration than those that arise at sites colocalizing with mitochondria but not associated with fission sites, and also those that arise at non-mitochondrial sites along the axon (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data in Figure 3E.

claim: Actin patches associated with mitochondria exhibited longer durations than those not associated with mitochondria regardless of whether they were associated with sites of fission.
source: Consistent with a prior report (Sainath et al., 2017a), actin patches associated with mitochondria exhibited longer durations than those not associated with mitochondria regardless of whether they were associated with sites of fission (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data in Figure 3E and a citation to prior work.

claim: Actin patches associated with mitochondria but not involved in fission exhibited an over 5-fold greater probability than patches associated with fission to give rise to a filopodium.
source: Actin patches associated with mitochondria but not involved in fission exhibited an over 5-fold greater probability than patches associated with fission to give rise to a filopodium (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data in Figure 3F.

claim: Patches associated with sites of fission generated filopodia with the same probability as patches not associated with mitochondria.
source: Patches associated with sites of fission generated filopodia with the same probability as patches not associated with mitochondria (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data in Figure 3F.

claim: Fission-associated actin patches represent a subpopulation of patches that colocalize with mitochondria and are specialized for fission and not the formation of filopodia.
source: These data indicate that fission-associated actin patches represent a subpopulation of patches that colocalize with mitochondria and are specialized for fission and not the formation of filopodia.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the differential properties of actin patches.

claim: Prior work addressing the cytoskeletal mechanism of actin patch formation underlying filopodia formation determined a role for the actin filament nucleating complex Arp2/3.
source: Prior work addressing the cytoskeletal mechanism of actin patch formation underlying filopodia formation determined a role for the actin filament nucleating complex Arp2/3 (Spillane et al., 2011; Spillane et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Pretreatment with an Arp2/3 inhibitor blocked the effects of NGF on mitochondria fission.
source: Pretreatment with an Arp2/3 inhibitor blocked the effects of NGF on mitochondria fission (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), indicating that although patches associated with fission sites differ from those involved in filopodia formation they share a conserved role for Arp2/3.
evidence: This claim is supported by pharmacological inhibition data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Patches associated with fission sites and those involved in filopodia formation share a conserved role for Arp2/3.
source: Pretreatment with an Arp2/3 inhibitor blocked the effects of NGF on mitochondria fission (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), indicating that although patches associated with fission sites differ from those involved in filopodia formation they share a conserved role for Arp2/3.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the Arp2/3 inhibition data.

claim: The PI3K and Mek-Erk pathways are major effectors of neurotrophin signaling and regulate neuronal morphogenesis.
source: The PI3K and Mek-Erk pathways are major effectors of neurotrophin signaling and regulate neuronal morphogenesis (Huang and Reichardt, 2003; Reichardt, 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Along axons, PI3K activity is required for mediating the effects of NGF on axonal actin patch formation.
source: Along axons, PI3K activity is required for mediating the effects of NGF on axonal actin patch formation (Ketschek and Gallo, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Phosphorylation of S616 in Drp1 enhances its activity and fission.
source: The activity of the Drp1 GTPase is under regulation by posttranslational modifications, and phosphorylation of S616 in Drp1 enhances its activity and fission (Hall et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Previous work showed that Erk phosphorylates Drp1 at S616 in cancer cells thereby promoting fission.
source: Additionally, previous work showed that Erk phosphorylates Drp1 at S616 in cancer cells thereby promoting fission (Kashatus et al., 2015; Serasinghe et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Inhibition of either PI3K or Mek-Erk signaling prevented the NGF-induced increase in mitochondria fission.
source: Inhibition of either PI3K or Mek-Erk signaling prevented the NGF-induced increase in mitochondria fission (Figure 4A) and also impaired the increase in Drp1 accumulations along mitochondria induced by NGF (Figure 4B), but did not impact fusion rates (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by pharmacological inhibition data in Figure 4A.

claim: Inhibition of either PI3K or Mek-Erk signaling impaired the increase in Drp1 accumulations along mitochondria induced by NGF.
source: Inhibition of either PI3K or Mek-Erk signaling prevented the NGF-induced increase in mitochondria fission (Figure 4A) and also impaired the increase in Drp1 accumulations along mitochondria induced by NGF (Figure 4B), but did not impact fusion rates (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data in Figure 4B.

claim: Inhibition of either PI3K or Mek-Erk signaling did not impact fusion rates.
source: Inhibition of either PI3K or Mek-Erk signaling prevented the NGF-induced increase in mitochondria fission (Figure 4A) and also impaired the increase in Drp1 accumulations along mitochondria induced by NGF (Figure 4B), but did not impact fusion rates (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: NGF induced increases in the levels of pS616-Drp1 along axons during the time of prominent fission (10 min post treatment).
source: NGF induced increases in the levels of pS16-Drp1 along axons during the time of prominent fission (10 min post treatment) (Figure 4C,D) without altering the axonal levels of total Drp1 protein (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunocytochemistry data in Figure 4C,D.

claim: NGF did not alter the axonal levels of total Drp1 protein.
source: NGF induced increases in the levels of pS16-Drp1 along axons during the time of prominent fission (10 min post treatment) (Figure 4C,D) without altering the axonal levels of total Drp1 protein (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Inhibition of PI3K had no effect on NGF-induced pS616 phosphorylation.
source: Inhibition of PI3K had no effect on NGF-induced pS616 phosphorylation (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data in Figure 4D.

claim: Inhibition of Mek-Erk signaling abolished the effects of NGF on pS616 levels.
source: In contrast, inhibition of Mek-Erk signaling abolished the effects of NGF on pS616 levels (Figure 4D) without affecting the levels of total Drp1 protein (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data in Figure 4D.

claim: Inhibition of Mek-Erk signaling did not affect the levels of total Drp1 protein.
source: In contrast, inhibition of Mek-Erk signaling abolished the effects of NGF on pS616 levels (Figure 4D) without affecting the levels of total Drp1 protein (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The Mek-Erk-dependent NGF-induced increases in pS616 levels correlated with the activation of Mek-Erk signaling in axons after NGF treatment.
source: The Mek-Erk-dependent NGF-induced increases in pS616 levels also correlated with the activation of Mek-Erk signaling in axons after NGF treatment (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data showing increased pErk levels in axons after NGF treatment.

claim: At 7.5 min after NGF the median levels of pErk in axons were elevated by 320%.
source: At 7.5 min after NGF the median levels of pErk in axons were elevated by 320%, and after 30 min and 1 hr of treatment levels were elevated by 134% and 67%, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data on pErk levels.

claim: The activity of PI3K in axons occurred within 2 min of NGF treatment and was most pronounced during the first 4–8 min of NGF treatment.
source: The activity of PI3K in axons, as reflected in the phosphorylation and activation of Akt (at T308), occurred within 2 min of NGF treatment and was most pronounced during the first 4–8 min of NGF treatment (maximal increase of approximately 450% above control levels at 6 min; Figure 4—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data on pAkt levels in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D,E.

claim: NGF elevated the activity of both PI3K-Akt and Erk pathways in axon segments containing mitochondria at 6 min of treatment when fission is occurring.
source: NGF elevated the activity of both pathways in axon segments containing mitochondria at 6 min of treatment when fission is occurring (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G-J).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1G-J.

claim: The Mek-Erk pathway regulates Drp1 activity through S616 phosphorylation independent of PI3K.
source: These data indicate that the Mek-Erk pathway regulates Drp1 activity through S616 phosphorylation independent of PI3K, both pathways contribute to the recruitment of Drp1 to focal accumulations along mitochondria, and the activation of the pathways is highest during the period of increased rates of fission and occurs within axon segments containing mitochondria.
evidence: This is a summary statement integrating multiple experimental findings.

claim: Both PI3K and Mek-Erk pathways contribute to the recruitment of Drp1 to focal accumulations along mitochondria.
source: These data indicate that the Mek-Erk pathway regulates Drp1 activity through S616 phosphorylation independent of PI3K, both pathways contribute to the recruitment of Drp1 to focal accumulations along mitochondria, and the activation of the pathways is highest during the period of increased rates of fission and occurs within axon segments containing mitochondria.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the data showing both pathways are required for Drp1 accumulation.

claim: Inhibition of either PI3K or Mek-Erk pathway increased mitochondria length during the NGF-induced steady state.
source: Inhibition of either pathway increased mitochondria length (Figure 4—figure supplement 1K) indicating both are required for the maintenance of the NGF-induced steady state.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1K.

claim: Both PI3K and Mek-Erk pathways are required for the maintenance of the NGF-induced steady state.
source: Inhibition of either pathway increased mitochondria length (Figure 4—figure supplement 1K) indicating both are required for the maintenance of the NGF-induced steady state.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data showing pathway inhibition increases mitochondrial length.

claim: Mitochondria have emerged as important mediators of axon branching.
source: Mitochondria have emerged as important mediators of axon branching (Courchet et al., 2013; Tao et al., 2014; Sainath et al., 2017a; Wong et al., 2017; Smith and Gallo, 2018), including NGF-induced branching (Spillane et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to recent literature.

claim: Branching in response to NGF treatment is statistically detectable at 15 min and maximal at 30 min.
source: Branching in response to NGF treatment is statistically detectable at 15 min and maximal at 30 min (Spillane et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The initial burst of fission in response to NGF occurs by <15 min post-treatment and by 15 min the new steady state of mitochondria density and length is established.
source: The initial burst of fission in response to NGF occurs by <15 min post-treatment and by 15 min the new steady state of mitochondria density and length is established.
evidence: This is a summary of the time-course data presented earlier in the manuscript.

claim: PI3K is involved in multiple aspects of the branching mechanism activated by NGF.
source: PI3K is involved in multiple aspects of the branching mechanism activated by NGF (Ketschek and Gallo, 2010; Spillane et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Inhibition of Mek-Erk signaling blocks NGF-induced branching.
source: Similarly, inhibition of Mek-Erk signaling also blocks NGF-induced branching (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Inhibition of Drp1 with mDivi-1, P110, or expression of DNDrp1 blocked NGF-induced axon branching.
source: Inhibition of Drp1 with mDivi-1, P110, or expression of DNDrp1 blocked NGF-induced axon branching (Figure 5A–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data in Figure 5A-D.

claim: Severing axons from the cell bodies does not alter branching in response to NGF.
source: As previously determined, severing axons from the cell bodies does not alter branching in response to NGF (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B) and treatment with mDivi-1 immediately after severing and prior to NGF application blocked NGF-induced axon branching (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This statement is supported by data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and references prior work.

claim: Treatment with mDivi-1 immediately after severing axons and prior to NGF application blocked NGF-induced axon branching.
source: As previously determined, severing axons from the cell bodies does not alter branching in response to NGF (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B) and treatment with mDivi-1 immediately after severing and prior to NGF application blocked NGF-induced axon branching (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Treatment with mDivi-1 did not alter the increases in growth cone size and number of growth cone filopodia induced by NGF.
source: In contrast to the requirement of fission for NGF-induced axon branching, treatment with mDivi-1 did not alter the increases in growth cone size and number of growth cone filopodia induced by NGF (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, D), indicating a role for fission specific to axon branching and not the regulation of growth cone morphology as previously also observed for NGF-induced intra-axonal protein synthesis (Roche et al., 2009; Spillane et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, D.

claim: Fission has a role specific to axon branching and not the regulation of growth cone morphology.
source: In contrast to the requirement of fission for NGF-induced axon branching, treatment with mDivi-1 did not alter the increases in growth cone size and number of growth cone filopodia induced by NGF (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, D), indicating a role for fission specific to axon branching and not the regulation of growth cone morphology as previously also observed for NGF-induced intra-axonal protein synthesis (Roche et al., 2009; Spillane et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the differential effects of mDivi-1 on branching versus growth cone morphology.

claim: The formation of axonal filopodia is the first step in the establishment of branches.
source: The formation of axonal filopodia is the first step in the establishment of branches (Kalil and Dent, 2014; Armijo-Weingart and Gallo, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: Actin patches formed along the axon serve as precursors to filopodia formation and NGF increases the rate of patch formation in a manner dependent on NGF-induced PI3K activity and intra-axonal protein synthesis.
source: Actin patches formed along the axon serve as precursors to filopodia formation and NGF increases the rate of patch formation in a manner dependent on NGF-induced PI3K activity and intra-axonal protein synthesis (Spillane et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: NGF increases the rate of filopodia formation but does not affect the probability that a patch will give rise to a filopodium.
source: NGF increases the rate of filopodia formation but does not affect the probability that a patch will give rise to a filopodium, and the increase in filopodia formation is due to the increase in patch formation (Ketschek and Gallo, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Increases in net actin patch formation rates are first detectable at 15–21 min post treatment and are further increased by 30–36 min.
source: Similar to the time course of NGF-induced branching, increases in net actin patch formation rates are first detectable at 15–21 min post treatment and are further increased by 30–36 min (Spillane et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Inhibition of fission using mDivi-1 blocked the NGF-induced increase in actin patch formation.
source: Analysis of the effects of a 30 min treatment with NGF on actin patches revealed that inhibition of fission using mDivi-1 blocked the NGF-induced increase in actin patch formation (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data in Figure 5E.

claim: Inhibition of fission did not alter patch duration or the probability of filopodial emergence from patches.
source: In contrast, inhibition of fission did not alter patch duration or the probability of filopodial emergence from patches (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E, F), two aspects of patch dynamics that are not under regulation by NGF (Ketschek and Gallo, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E, F.

claim: Inhibition of Erk blocked the NGF-induced increase in the rate of actin patch formation.
source: Inhibition of Mek-Erk blocked the NGF-induced increase in the rate of actin patch formation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1G), an observation consistent with the inhibition and requirement for fission detailed above but not excluding the involvement of Erk in other mechanisms.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1G.

claim: In NGF treatment conditions, the lengths of mitochondria in branches were not different than those along the main axons shaft.
source: In NGF treatment conditions, the lengths of mitochondria in branches were not different that those along the main axons shaft (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data in Figure 5F.

claim: In the absence of NGF treatment mitochondria in branches that formed without NGF stimulation were shorter than in the axon shaft.
source: In contrast, in the absence of NGF treatment mitochondria in branches that formed without NGF stimulation were shorter than in the axon shaft (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data in Figure 5F.

claim: The lengths of mitochondria targeted to branches formed in the absence of NGF were of similar lengths to those found in axons, and branches, after NGF treatment.
source: Furthermore, the lengths of mitochondria targeted to branches formed in the absence of NGF were of similar lengths to those found in axons, and branches, after NGF treatment.
evidence: This is an observation based on comparison of mitochondrial lengths in different conditions.

claim: NGF-induced branches exhibited increased densities of mitochondria relative to branches formed in the absence of NGF.
source: NGF-induced branches also exhibited increased densities of mitochondria relative to branches formed in the absence of NGF (Figure 5G).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data in Figure 5G.

claim: NGF-induced fission generates a population of mitochondria that have facilitated access to nascent branches.
source: This observation indicates that NGF-induced fission generates a population of mitochondria that have facilitated access to nascent branches.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observation that mitochondria in branches have similar lengths to those in axons after NGF treatment.

claim: Both exogenous and endogenous NGF can induce branching of sensory axons in vivo in the adult spinal cord.
source: Both exogenous and endogenous NGF can induce branching of sensory axons in vivo in the adult spinal cord (Brown and Weaver, 2012; Keefe et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: NGF does not control the formation of sensory axon collateral branches in the developing spinal cord.
source: However, NGF does not control the formation of sensory axon collateral branches in the developing spinal cord (Patel et al., 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Expression of DNDrp1 increased the lengths of mitochondria in axons extending in the spinal cord.
source: Expression of DNDrp1 increased the lengths of mitochondria in axons extending in the spinal cord (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data in Figure 6A,B.

claim: The mean total 'mass' of mitochondria was 2.67 and 5.47 for control and DNDrp1 groups.
source: The mean total 'mass' of mitochondria (mean length X mean density/10 μm) was 2.67 and 5.47 for control and DNDrp1 groups (using the data presented in Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a calculated value based on the data in Figure 6B.

claim: An increase of total mass of mitochondria in axons when fission is impaired in vivo is consistent with a recent report focusing on cortical neurons in vivo.
source: An increase of total mass of mitochondria in axons when fission is impaired in vivo is consistent with a recent report focusing on cortical neurons in vivo (Lewis et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement compares the current findings to a prior study.

claim: Analysis of branching along the axons of neurons expressing DNDrp1 revealed decreased density of branches.
source: Analysis of branching along the axons of neurons expressing DNDrp1 revealed decreased density of branches (Figure 6C,D), indicating the regulation of mitochondria length and density by fission is also required for non-neurotrophin dependent branching during development.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data in Figure 6C,D.

claim: The regulation of mitochondria length and density by fission is required for non-neurotrophin dependent branching during development.
source: Analysis of branching along the axons of neurons expressing DNDrp1 revealed decreased density of branches (Figure 6C,D), indicating the regulation of mitochondria length and density by fission is also required for non-neurotrophin dependent branching during development.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the in vivo data showing DNDrp1 impairs developmental branching.

claim: The median length of E14 mitochondria was increased by 33% relative to that of E7.
source: Furthermore, the length of mitochondria a and b at 12 s, during overlap, were 2.14 and 10.66 μm respectively. At 24 s and later the length of the fused mitochondrion (a+b) was 12.82 μm.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative comparison of mitochondrial lengths at different developmental stages.

claim: The induction of axon branches and increase in the formation of axonal actin patches by NGF are dependent on NGF-induced intra-axonal protein synthesis of Arp2/3 regulators and Arp2/3 subunits.
source: The induction of axon branches and increase in the formation of axonal actin patches by NGF are dependent on NGF-induced intra-axonal protein synthesis of Arp2/3 regulators and Arp2/3 subunits (Spillane et al., 2012; Spillane et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Inhibition of fission using mDivi-1 prior to NGF treatment attenuated the translation of myrGFP-cortactin 3'UTR.
source: Live imaging of the FRAP of myrGFP-cortactin 3'UTR in axons after photobleaching showed that inhibition of fission using mDivi-1 prior to NGF treatment attenuated the translation of myrGFP-cortactin 3'UTR (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by FRAP data in Figure 7A,B.

claim: NGF treatment increases the protein levels of cortactin protein in axons in a manner dependent on intra-axonal protein synthesis.
source: As demonstrated by quantitative immunocytochemistry, NGF treatment also increases the protein levels of cortactin protein in axons in a manner dependent on intra-axonal protein synthesis (Spillane et al., 2013; Ketschek et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Inhibition of fission blocked the NGF-induced increase in the axonal levels of cortactin.
source: Inhibition of fission blocked the NGF-induced increase in the axonal levels of cortactin (Figure 7C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunocytochemistry data in Figure 7C,D.

claim: PI3K signaling is required for the NGF-induced intra-axonal translation dependent increase in axonal levels of cortactin.
source: We have previously reported the requirement for PI3K signaling in the NGF-induced intra-axonal translation dependent increase in axonal levels of cortactin (Spillane et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement references prior work by the authors.

claim: Inhibition of Mek-Erk signaling attenuated the NGF-induced increase in cortactin axonal protein levels.
source: Inhibition of Mek-Erk signaling attenuated the NGF-induced increase in cortactin axonal protein levels (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The fission of mitochondria in response to NGF is required to mount the intra-axonal protein synthesis of cortactin that is in turn required for NGF-induced branching.
source: These data indicate that the fission of mitochondria in response to NGF is required to mount the intra-axonal protein synthesis of cortactin that is in turn required for NGF-induced branching.
evidence: This is a summary statement integrating multiple experimental findings.

claim: Pretreatment with the translational inhibitor cycloheximide did not impact the change in mitochondria length induced by NGF.
source: Pretreatment with the translational inhibitor cycloheximide, which blocks NGF-induced axonal protein synthesis and branching (Spillane et al., 2012), did not impact the change in mitochondria length induced by NGF (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: While NGF-induced mitochondria fission contributes to establishing NGF-induced intra-axonal translation the latter is not required for the former.
source: Collectively, the data indicate that while NGF-induced mitochondria fission contributes to establishing NGF-induced intra-axonal translation the latter is not required for the former.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observation that translation inhibition does not affect fission.

claim: This study unveils a novel biological function of neurotrophins; the regulation of mitochondrial fission and steady state mitochondrial length and density in axons.
source: Collectively, these observations unveil a novel biological function of neurotrophins; the regulation of mitochondrial fission and steady state mitochondrial length and density in axons.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the major finding of the study.

claim: This study provides the first example of the 'beneficial' regulation of mitochondria fission by a family of neuronal growth factors.
source: This study thus unveils a novel biological function of neurotrophins, the induction of mitochondrial fission and maintenance of steady state mitochondrial length and density in axons, and provides the first example of the 'beneficial' regulation of mitochondria fission by a family of neuronal growth factors.
evidence: This is a summary statement highlighting the novelty of the findings.

claim: The mechanism of fission used by neurotrophins is Drp1 dependent, as with other forms of fission.
source: The mechanism of fission used by neurotrophins is Drp1 dependent, as with other forms of fission (Kraus and Ryan, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by the experimental data and a citation to prior literature.

claim: A role for growth factor signaling in fission has not been reported.
source: The field of mitochondria fission has relied on the analysis of spontaneously occurring fission or fission induced by impairing mitochondrial function (e.g., using mitochondrial poisons). A role for growth factor signaling in fission has not been reported.
evidence: This statement reflects the novelty of the current findings in the context of the existing literature.

claim: This study reveals a role for actin filaments in fission, consistent with an emerging literature.
source: This study reveals a role for actin filaments in fission, consistent with an emerging literature (Hatch et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by the experimental data and a citation to prior literature.

claim: This study unveils a novel role for axonal actin patches, their involvement in fission, independent of their previously described role in the formation of axonal filopodia.
source: Moreover, in the case of neurotrophin signaling, we were able to observe the formation of discrete actin patches at sites of fission. This observation unveils a novel role for axonal actin patches, their involvement in fission, independent of their previously described role in the formation of axonal filopodia that represents the first step in the sequence of morphological changes leading to axon collateral branching (reviewed in Armijo-Weingart and Gallo, 2017).
evidence: This is a summary statement highlighting a novel finding of the study.

claim: For the population of patches that form associated with mitochondria there are two distinct subpopulations with dedicated roles in the formation of filopodia and fission, respectively.
source: Furthermore, the data show that even for the population of patches that form associated with mitochondria there are two distinct subpopulations with dedicated roles in the formation of filopodia and fission, respectively.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the differential properties of actin patches associated with mitochondria.

claim: A role for PI3K signaling in regulating Drp1-dependent mitochondria fission has not been previously reported.
source: A role for PI3K signaling in regulating Drp1-dependent mitochondria fission has not been previously reported.
evidence: This statement highlights the novelty of the finding regarding PI3K's role in fission.

claim: PI3K signaling, unlike Mek-Erk, does not regulate the activation of Drp1 through S616 phosphorylation.
source: PI3K signaling, unlike Mek-Erk, does not regulate the activation of Drp1 through S616 phosphorylation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data showing PI3K inhibition does not affect pS616 levels.

claim: PI3K controls the actin patch dependent aspect of the fission mechanism.
source: Given the previously detailed role of PI3K in establishing local signaling microdomains in axons that determine the localized formation and elaboration of axonal actin patches that in turn colocalize with mitochondria (Ketschek and Gallo, 2010), the role of actin patches in fission and the dependence of both fission and actin patch formation on PI3K and Arp2/3, we propose that PI3K controls the actin patch dependent aspect of the fission mechanism (Figure 8A), but do not exclude alternative mechanisms.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on integration of current and prior findings.

claim: The INF2 formin has been shown to mediate ER-mitochondria contact mediated fission.
source: For example, the INF2 formin has been shown to mediate ER-mitochondria contact mediated fission (Korobova et al., 2013) and mitochondria and the ER both accumulate at sites of axon branching (Spillane et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Mitochondria and the ER both accumulate at sites of axon branching.
source: For example, the INF2 formin has been shown to mediate ER-mitochondria contact mediated fission (Korobova et al., 2013) and mitochondria and the ER both accumulate at sites of axon branching (Spillane et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: NGF-induced fission is required for the ensuing collateral branching.
source: NGF-induced fission is required for the ensuing collateral branching, and inhibition of Drp1 in vivo impairs developmental collateral axon branching in the embryonic spinal cord although this branching is not initiated by NGF (Patel et al., 2000).
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the experimental data.

claim: A recent study reports that inhibition of mitochondria fission through depletion of MFF decreases the terminal/collateral branching of cortical axons in vivo.
source: Similarly, a recent study reports that inhibition of mitochondria fission through depletion of MFF, one of the Drp1 adaptors on the mitochondrial surface, decreases the terminal/collateral branching of cortical axons in vivo (Lewis et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a recent study.

claim: The current study provides insights into the contribution of mitochondria fission through the regulation of mitochondria length and density to the mechanism of branching, independent of the specific signal initiating the branching.
source: The current study provides insights into the contribution of mitochondria fission through the regulation of mitochondria length and density to the mechanism of branching, independent of the specific signal initiating the branching.
evidence: This is a summary statement highlighting the broader implications of the findings.

claim: The data reveal a 'size principle' for the targeting of mitochondria into nascent branches.
source: The data reveal a 'size principle' for the targeting of mitochondria into nascent branches.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observation that shorter mitochondria preferentially enter branches.

claim: In the absence of neurotrophins, only the few available short mitochondria target into spontaneously formed branches.
source: In the absence of neurotrophins, only the few available short mitochondria target into spontaneously formed branches.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data on mitochondrial lengths in branches.

claim: Neurotrophins greatly increase the availability of mitochondria in the size range appropriate for branch formation and maturation.
source: The size of these mitochondria that enter branches in the absence of NGF is similar to the size induced by neurotrophins throughout the axon following fission, indicating that neurotrophins greatly increase the availability of mitochondria in the size range appropriate for branch formation and maturation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the comparison of mitochondrial sizes in different conditions.

claim: Li et al. (2004) reported that small mitochondria tend to target to dendritic filopodia and spines.
source: Li et al. (2004) similarly reported that small mitochondria tend to target to dendritic filopodia and spines, although they also observed portions of larger mitochondria penetrating dendritic protrusions.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: When axonal mitochondria undergo fission, regardless of NGF treatment, one or both of the emergent mitochondria undergo transport.
source: Furthermore, the data show that when axonal mitochondria undergo fission, regardless of NGF treatment, one or both of the emergent mitochondria undergo transport.
evidence: This is a summary of the data on mitochondrial transport after fission.

claim: An inverse relationship between the length of axonal mitochondria and their propensity for undergoing transport has been reported.
source: While the mechanism that links fission with subsequent transport is not clear, an inverse relationship between the length of axonal mitochondria and their propensity for undergoing transport has been reported (Saxton and Hollenbeck, 2012; Narayanareddy et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The length of mitochondria is dependent on the balance of fission and fusion.
source: The length of mitochondria is dependent on the balance of fission and fusion.
evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge about mitochondrial dynamics.

claim: Branches emerge from sites along the axon where mitochondria have undergone stalling.
source: Branches emerge from sites along the axon where mitochondria have undergone stalling (Courchet et al., 2013; Spillane et al., 2013; Tao et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: One role of fission is to promote the reorganization of the distribution of axonal mitochondria allowing them to target to sites of future branching.
source: Thus, we suggest that one role of fission is to promote the reorganization of the distribution of axonal mitochondria allowing them the target to sites of future branching.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on integration of current and prior findings.

claim: Sites of branching are characterized by localized splaying of the axonal microtubule array.
source: Sites of branching are characterized by localized splaying of the axonal microtubule array (Dent and Kalil, 2001; Ketschek et al., 2015) and NGF promotes the splaying by 5 min after treatment (Ketschek et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: NGF promotes microtubule splaying by 5 min after treatment.
source: Sites of branching are characterized by localized splaying of the axonal microtubule array (Dent and Kalil, 2001; Ketschek et al., 2015) and NGF promotes the splaying by 5 min after treatment (Ketschek et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Sites of microtubule splaying may serve to locally capture mitochondria in transit.
source: Thus, as mitochondria are undergoing redistribution within the axon following NGF-induced fission they will encounter sites of microtubule splaying that we suggest may serve to locally capture mitochondria in transit, and lead to the observed accumulation of mitochondria and other organelles at the base of nascent branches (Yu et al., 1994; Courchet et al., 2013; Spillane et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on integration of current and prior findings.

claim: Through their respiration stalled mitochondria establish sites of localized high axonal mRNA translation that correlate with sites of axon branching and are required for the ensuing branching.
source: Through their respiration stalled mitochondria also establish sites of localized high axonal mRNA translation that correlate with sites of axon branching and are required for the ensuing branching (Spillane et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Sites of axon branching accumulate ribosomal RNA.
source: Sites of axon branching have also been shown to accumulate ribosomal RNA (Spillane et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The orchestration in space and time of the accumulation of mitochondria and translational machinery at sites of axon collateral branching has been demonstrated in vivo along retinal ganglion cell axons.
source: Furthermore, the orchestration in space and time of the accumulation of mitochondria and translational machinery at sites of axon collateral branching has been demonstrated in vivo along retinal ganglion cell axons (Wong et al., 2017) whose collateral branches are under regulation by BDNF (Cohen-Cory et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Retinal ganglion cell axon collateral branches are under regulation by BDNF.
source: Furthermore, the orchestration in space and time of the accumulation of mitochondria and translational machinery at sites of axon collateral branching has been demonstrated in vivo along retinal ganglion cell axons (Wong et al., 2017) whose collateral branches are under regulation by BDNF (Cohen-Cory et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Wong et al. (2017) determined that both mitochondria and translational machinery stall at specific sites along axons.
source: The study by Wong et al. (2017) determined that both mitochondria and translational machinery stall at specific sites along axons supporting the idea that axons have specific sites that capture the relevant machinery (e.g., possibly sites marked by microtubule splaying).
